name: Zygomatic reduction

lead: Zygomatic reduction, also called malarplasty or cheekbone shaving, reshapes or repositions the cheekbones to give a narrower or flatter midface. People with a wide or prominent midface seek it for a slimmer facial width.

The cheek bone is cut and reshaped or moved inward, as forum posters describe it; some say shaving mainly reduces forward projection rather than width. On looksmax.org users debate whether width comes from bone or fat and whether the surgery improves proportions. The wiki's sources contain no outcome studies.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done under anaesthesia by a facial or plastic surgeon, popular in Asian aesthetic surgery. Swelling settles over weeks, and the final shape is judged after healing.
It is a bone-cutting operation under anaesthesia. Forum members report results ranging from very good to very bad, and no complication data were available in the sources used here.

angle.text: People with a wide or prominent midface want a narrower, slimmer facial width. The cheekbone is shaved or repositioned inward, so the change is visible after healing. Forum members report mixed before-and-after outcomes.

lead: Zygomatic reduction, also called reduction malarplasty, cheekbone reduction or cheekbone shaving, is surgery that narrows or lowers the projection of the cheekbones (the zygomatic bones) to give a slimmer, more oval facial outline.[1][2] People pursue it to reduce a wide midface, soften prominent cheek angles and balance the face against the jaw and forehead.[3]

The operation is most associated with East Asia, where an oval or 'melon seed' face is considered delicate and attractive and cosmetic bone contouring has become increasingly popular; requests have also been rising in the United States.[1][3] Techniques include L-shaped osteotomy, in which the zygomatic body and arch are cut, repositioned medially and fixed with screws, often through incisions inside the mouth and a small incision by the sideburn.[4]

Published work is mainly surgical technique series and reviews. A 2023 meta-analysis pooled 29 studies and 6,611 patients to compare complications among reduction malarplasty methods.[5] On looksmax.org, members discuss it in relation to face width, eye-to-eye spacing ratio and facial harmony, with before-and-after examples cited on both sides.[6][7]

paras: The zygomatic bone forms the cheekbone and part of the orbital wall. A review of skeletal contouring in ethnic patients states that the zygomaticomaxillary complex and mandible shape how overlying soft tissue is draped and lit, that their projection is sexually dimorphic and ethnically defined, and that excessive projection in any dimension can look undesirable to some patients.[3]

Cultural ideals vary: a cosmetic bone contouring review notes that in some cultures a wide jaw and a square face are considered less attractive while an oval face is viewed as feminine and delicate.[1]

Reduction malarplasty has been described in the plastic surgery literature since at least the early 1990s.[8][9] One L-shaped osteotomy technique through intraoral and sideburn incisions removes a middle segment of the anterior zygomatic body, fractures the arch root, and repositions the freed complex medially with one or two screws; a series of 32 patients reported simple manipulation, stable fixation and less risk of a drooping face.[4]

Newer work describes digital planning, augmented reality and robot-assisted techniques in facial bone contouring, and an intraoral skeletal contouring simulator for surgeon training.[10][11] A three-dimensional CT study of 80 patients after L-shaped malarplasty found that bone setback or resection correlated with changes in anterior and middle zygomatic width and protrusion, and the authors proposed a regression equation to help preoperative planning.[12]

The 2023 meta-analysis found that L-shaped osteotomy without bony resection had the lowest postoperative complication incidence (0.02%) but limits how much bone can be removed; with larger resections, long-arm resection had the fewest structural complications and short-arm the fewest functional ones.[5] Case reports describe maxillary sinusitis after the operation, including two cases treated with endoscopic sinus surgery.[13]

Because blood supply to the maxillofacial area is abundant and the intraoral field is narrow, hemostasis is a recognized challenge in facial contouring surgery; a randomized study of 282 patients evaluated a soluble hemostatic gauze.[14]

Evidence consists of surgical technique reports, reviews and observational series. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 studies (6,611 patients) compared complications across reduction malarplasty methods.[5] A retrospective 3D CT study of 80 patients measured zygomatic width and protrusion changes after L-shaped malarplasty.[12] A 32-patient technique series reported outcomes of one L-shaped osteotomy approach.[4] No randomized trial comparing surgery with no surgery on appearance was identified.

lore.intro: Forum members discuss cheekbone shaving mainly for wide faces and as a way to change facial ratios, and they trade before-and-after examples.[6][7]

claims.claim: Cheekbone shaving mainly reduces forward projection, not width.
It can ascend a wide face but can harm a well-proportioned one.
Cheekbone surgery can raise the eye-to-eye spacing ratio (ESR).
